attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of what is known about Big Five personality traits in EFL (and closely related ESL/TEFL) teachers, drawing on EFL-specific studies and meta-analytic evidence from teacher populations.

1) Big Five constructs and why they matter for EFL teachers
- The Big Five model captures five broad dimensions—openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and emotional stability/neuroticism—that have widespread cross-cultural support and robust psychometric tools (e.g., BFI) used across education and psychology, including language teaching contexts.<cite id="de928b43-4">The Big Five model has functioned as a powerful theoretical framework to synthesize most of the variation in relatively stable patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, with roots in psycho-lexical and questionnaire approaches that emphasize universality and synonym frequency for trait terms</cite><cite id="de928b43-4">The Big Five Inventory is a short, validated instrument (44 items) widely used to assess the five domains with acceptable internal consistency</cite>. 
- In language education, researchers have applied the Big Five to EFL/ESL teacher populations to study links with reflective practice and communication capacities central to EFL teaching.<cite id="de928b43-0">Studies of Iranian EFL teachers have explicitly examined relationships between Big Five traits and reflective teaching</cite><cite id="de928b43-3">Among Malaysian TESL trainees, Big Five traits were investigated in relation to verbal communication skills (interpersonal, verbal-linguistic, motivation, altruism, self-regulation)</cite>.

2) Meta-analytic patterns: which traits predict teacher effectiveness and well-being
- A meta-analysis of 25 studies (N=6,294) directly testing Big Five domains against teacher effectiveness and burnout found that, with one exception, Big Five domains relate positively to effectiveness, especially when evaluated via classroom observation and student ratings; emotional stability (low neuroticism), extraversion, and conscientiousness also associate with lower burnout; and other-reported personality (peers/students/administrators) tends to predict outcomes more strongly than self-reports.<cite id="f541902e-1">Teacher Big Five domains (except agreeableness) were positively associated with teacher effectiveness, especially for evaluations of teaching; emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness were negatively associated with burnout; other-reports of personality were more strongly associated with outcomes than self-reports</cite><cite id="f541902e-0">The meta-analysis synthesized 25 studies on teacher Big Five and two outcomes (effectiveness and burnout), addressing moderators such as measure type (student performance self-efficacy, classroom observation, academic achievement, teaching evaluations) and source of personality report</cite>. 
- Integrative reviews in teacher psychology similarly conclude that Big Five-based personality correlates positively with effectiveness at small-to-trivial average effect sizes, while also noting links to stress susceptibility that vary by personality structure.<cite id="f541902e-4">Across teacher studies, personality composites (including Big Five-derived indicators) show a small-to-trivial average positive relation to teacher effectiveness (student achievement and observer ratings), and stress-focused meta-analytic work argues some profiles may be more predisposed to stress due to personality</cite>. 
- Taken together, these results imply a practical profile for effective EFL teachers likely showing higher openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion, and lower neuroticism, with mixed or smaller associations for agreeableness depending on outcome and method; student/classroom ratings carry more weight than self-ratings when linking traits to effectiveness.<cite id="f541902e-1">Effectiveness associations are strongest for evaluations of teaching; emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness relate negatively to burnout; other-reports outperform self-reports</cite><cite id="f541902e-4">Big Five covers extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and emotional stability as the core dimensions used in teacher effectiveness syntheses</cite>.

3) What EFL/ESL-specific studies show (mechanisms, moderators, and cultural notes)
- Iranian EFL teachers: Trait–reflective practice links are specific and informative. Openness and conscientiousness correlate positively with reflective behavior, while neuroticism relates negatively; extraversion and agreeableness do not correlate with reflective teaching in this sample. The study also notes that extraverted teachers more often draw on the affective element in teaching, suggesting an emotional-contagion and rapport facet of classroom practice.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Among Iranian EFL teachers, openness and conscientiousness positively related to reflectivity, while neuroticism negatively related; agreeableness and extraversion did not correlate with reflectivity</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-1">Extrovert teachers were found to draw on the affective element in their teaching practices</cite>. 
- Cross-culturally, similar mechanisms emerge in pre-service EFL/ESL educators. In Malaysian TESL trainees, only openness showed a positive relationship with verbal communication skills (interpersonal, linguistic, altruism, self-regulation, motivation), underscoring the centrality of openness-related curiosity and sociolinguistic sensitivity to communicative teaching behaviors.<cite id="de928b43-3">Only openness positively related to verbal communication skills among TESL trainees, highlighting its importance for interpersonal and linguistic pedagogical behaviors</cite>. 
- Background syntheses highlight that reflective practice is a core driver of professional growth in language teaching, and they motivate targeted measurement of Big Five in teacher selection and development as reflective teachers show better self-regulation and coping, with personality-linked differences in how teachers approach reflective tasks.<cite id="4b4edf05-3">Reflection is core to sustaining effective professional development in teacher education; understanding connections between Big Five traits and teacher reflection can inform selection and professional growth</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-4">Personality traits influence how teachers reflect on methods and strategies, indicating that personalities affect teaching perspectives and responses to stressors</cite>. 
- Measurement notes matter in EFL/ESL contexts. Studies in teacher training commonly adapt validated BFI or Chinese-language Big Five instruments with good reliability, which supports cross-cultural comparability when scales are localized and rigorously validated.<cite id="2dcc5d99-0">The Chinese Big Five Personality Inventory-15 measures the five domains with acceptable internal consistency (alpha ≈ 0.74–0.84)</cite><cite id="de928b43-2">Adapted BFI among prospective teachers showed internal consistencies per domain of 0.62–0.75 with overall reliability 0.79</cite><cite id="2dcc5d99-4">Chinese versions of BFI demonstrate good reliability and validity for university populations</cite>.

4) Practical implications for EFL teacher selection, development, and evaluation
- Targeted traits for development: Evidence converges on the importance of cultivating openness (curiosity, cultural awareness), conscientiousness (planning, reliability), and extraversion (presence, rapport, engagement), and on screening/mitigating high neuroticism through coaching and reflective practice to reduce burnout risk, particularly in high-stakes EFL contexts.<cite id="f541902e-1">Openness, conscientiousness, and agreeableness relate positively to effectiveness (except agreeableness in some analyses), while emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness relate to lower burnout</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-2">Openness and conscientiousness enhance reflective reactions and workplace behavior, whereas neuroticism impairs reflective behavior</cite>. 
- Use multi-rater assessments: Because other-reported personality correlates more strongly with outcomes than self-reports, incorporating student/classroom observations and peer feedback into pre- and in-service evaluations can better identify trait-related strengths and risks for EFL teachers.<cite id="f541902e-1">Other-reports of teacher personality were more strongly associated with outcomes than self-reports</cite>. 
- Design reflective practice to fit personality: In EFL teams, match teachers to reflection formats (e.g., affective-focused debriefs for extraverted teachers; structured cognitive strategies for conscientious/open teachers) and provide support for neurotic teachers to build self-regulation and coping for sustained impact.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Each Big Five trait (except extraversion and agreeableness) shaped reflective behaviors; neuroticism required targeted strategies to modify behavior, while openness and conscientiousness supported better reactions and behavior</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-3">Reflective teachers better cope with challenges and improve teaching quality, suggesting tailored development can leverage personality–reflection linkages</cite>. 
- Anticipate heterogeneity and limits: Agreeableness shows weaker or inconsistent links to effectiveness across teacher meta-analyses, and some Big Five–outcome associations are small-to-trivial; EFL-specific effects can vary by sample and measure, so avoid overgeneralization and monitor outcomes locally.<cite id="f541902e-1">Except for agreeableness, other Big Five domains related to effectiveness; effect sizes can depend on measure type and source of ratings</cite><cite id="f541902e-4">Average effects of personality composites on teacher effectiveness are small-to-trivial, underscoring contextual moderation</cite>.

5) What remains uncertain or under-studied in EFL
- EFL teacher “profiles”: While EFL/ESL studies show trait–teaching behavior links (reflectivity, communication) and meta-analyses generalize to teacher effectiveness, there are few cross-country EFL-wide profiles with standardized, multi-rater outcomes. Iranian and Malaysian samples suggest convergent patterns (openness and conscientiousness beneficial; neuroticism detrimental), but more diverse EFL contexts and in-service cohorts are needed.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Openness, conscientiousness, and neuroticism showed consistent relationships with reflective behaviors among Iranian EFL teachers</cite><cite id="de928b43-3">Openness uniquely predicted verbal communication skills in Malaysian TESL trainees</cite>. 
- Mechanisms and cultural moderation: How cross-cultural EFL constraints (e.g., large classes, scripted curricula, test-centered accountability) interact with Big Five (e.g., extraversion’s effectiveness may differ in low-interactive settings) is underexplored; studies call for replication with varied experience levels, gender, language proficiency, and affective skills.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Future work should examine teachers with different personalities and teaching experiences and consider individual attributes and language skills</cite><cite id="f541902e-1">Moderators include source of personality report and effectiveness measure type, suggesting context matters</cite>. 
- Measurement: Although Chinese and English-language BFI derivatives have good reliability, localized adaptations to EFL-specific teaching values and idioms are still emerging; triangulation with classroom observation and student performance self-efficacy is recommended to avoid construct drift.<cite id="2dcc5d99-0">Chinese Big Five short and full scales show acceptable reliability and brevity for classroom use</cite><cite id="f541902e-1">Student ratings, observation, and achievement-based measures differentially moderate Big Five–effectiveness links</cite>.

6) Bottom line profile for EFL teachers
- Strengths to cultivate: Openness (curiosity, intercultural sensitivity), conscientiousness (preparation, follow-through), and extraversion (engagement, rapport) are generally associated with stronger classroom evaluations and lower burnout, and they align with observed EFL teaching behaviors like reflective practice and communicative skill development.<cite id="f541902e-1">Openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion relate positively to teacher effectiveness and lower burnout</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-2">Openness and conscientiousness enhanced reflective behaviors and workplace responses</cite><cite id="de928b43-3">Openness uniquely predicted verbal communication skills in TESL trainees</cite>. 
- Risks to mitigate: High neuroticism impairs reflective capacity and can undermine well-being; targeted reflective practice, coaching, and supportive school climates can buffer these risks in EFL settings.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Neuroticism related negatively to reflectivity, whereas openness and conscientiousness supported positive behaviors</cite><cite id="f541902e-1">Emotional stability related negatively to burnout</cite>. 
- Mixed/conditional findings: Agreeableness shows weaker or inconsistent links to effectiveness across teacher meta-analyses; effects for specific Big Five traits can be small and vary by rating source and outcome definition, so EFL programs should integrate Big Five insights with classroom-based evidence and professional development rather than rely on traits alone.<cite id="f541902e-1">Agreeableness did not show the positive effectiveness relation seen for other traits; other-reports outperform self-reports</cite><cite id="f541902e-4">Personality composite effects on effectiveness are small-to-trivial on average, underscoring the need for applied, context-sensitive use</cite>.

Practical takeaway: Use validated Big Five assessments adapted to local languages with multi-rater feedback (students, peers, supervisors), pair trait insights with classroom observation rubrics and reflective coaching, and prioritize development plans that leverage teachers’ strengths (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion) while providing targeted support for emotional regulation and self-efficacy in teachers with higher neuroticism.<cite id="f541902e-1">Other-reports and classroom-based effectiveness measures strengthen inference about trait–outcome links</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-3">Reflective practice is central to professional development, and personality–reflection linkages can guide tailored interventions</cite>.

Snippet: In response to increasing attention on understanding the teacher personal characteristics associated with job-related outcomes (e.g., Sutcher et al. 2016), various meta-analyses on teacher factors have been conducted (e.g., Brown 2012;Mérida-López and Extremera 2017;Visible Learning Plus 2018). Title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
Snippet: The question of what makes a good teacher has been asked by practitioners, policymakers, and researchers for decades. However, there is no guiding framework about which qualities are important for teachers. Thus, it is necessary to examine these qualities using a recognized framework and to summarize the previous literature on this topic. We conducted a meta-analysis on the 25 studies (total N = 6294) reporting the relationships between teacher Big Five personality domains (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and emotional stability) and two teacher job-related outcomes (i.e., teacher effectiveness and burnout). Furthermore, the influence of three moderators was assessed, namely, the type of teacher effectiveness measure (i.e., evaluations of teaching, student performance self-efficacy, classroom observation, and academic achievement), source of personality report (i.e., self-report vs other-report), and the instructed educational level (i.e., elementary, secondary, and tertiary). Overall, teacher Big Five domains (except for agreeableness) were positively associated with teacher effectiveness, especially for evaluations of teaching. Furthermore, teacher emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness were negatively associated with burnout. Other-reports of teacher personality were more strongly associated with outcomes than self-reports. There were no differences in the strength of the associations between the educational levels. The need for using common descriptors in teacher research as well as practical implications of the findings for teacher personality measurement is discussed.

Title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
Snippet: Our systematic literature search used three search strategies to identify all relevant literature concerning the relationship between teacher Big Five personality domains and the two jobrelated outcomes. First, we conducted an electronic search of the relevant articles using different databases relevant to our particular topic: PsycINFO (for psychological research and related fields), ERIC (for educational research), Web of Science (referencing science of all kinds), and Proquest Theses and Dissertations Global (in order to include unpublished literature and avoid publication bias). For our electronic search, we developed the following search term: (Bteacher personality^OR Bpersonality of teacher OR health OR well-being OR efficacy). We searched for articles with no date restrictions as well as both peer-reviewed and non-peer-reviewed articles to reduce the chance of including articles with publication biases. Second, we examined Klassen and Tze's (2014) meta-analysis for studies they included on teacher personality and teacher effectiveness. Third, we examined studies citing Klassen and Tze's meta-analysis. 

The electronic search resulted in a total of 1121 abstracts (PsycINFO 551 articles, Web of Science 90 articles, Proquest Dissertation Global 256 articles, ERIC 324 articles) and 11 additional studies. In the first step, we excluded 738 records. We excluded studies that were not applicable to the current meta-analysis, including expert opinions, theoretical discussions, and qualitative data. We also excluded studies reporting relationships not associated with our research questions, including studies on perspectives of students' teacher personality preferences and on the associations between student personality and educational outcomes. This process led to further examining 129 studies. The flow diagram (see Fig. 1) illustrates our process through the different phases.

Title: Teachers’ Psychological Characteristics: Do They Matter for Teacher Effectiveness, Teachers’ Well-being, Retention, and Interpersonal Relations? An Integrative Review
Snippet: Personality characteristics-often referred to as relatively enduring patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors (e.g., Roberts & Jackson, 2008)-have been subject to several metaanalyses and systematic reviews in the teacher domain. Klassen and Tze (2014) metaanalytically summarized the relationship between in-service and pre-service teachers' personality and teacher effectiveness assessed by student achievement and external observer ratings. Of the twelve included studies, five relied on the Big Five framework, two on the Myers-Briggs framework, and five on other personality measures that were not further described by the authors. The Big Five framework, as the most well-known personality framework, covers five basic dimensions of personality: extraversion (active, assertive social), openness (openminded, curious, cultured), agreeableness (altruistic, tender-minded, cooperative), conscientiousness (self-controlled, following norms and rules, organized), and emotional stability (calm, not neurotic) (see, e.g., John et al., 2008 for an overview). The Myers-Briggs framework contains sixteen different personality types which result from combinations of four attitudes or orientations (extraversion vs. introversion, and judging vs. perceiving) and four functions (sensing vs. intuition, and thinking vs. feeling) (e.g., Myers, 1998). In their metaanalysis, Klassen and Tze (2014) did not differentiate between different personality constructs (e.g., specific Big Five dimensions, such as conscientiousness and extraversion, or Myer-Briggs personality types) and instead treated all constructs as indicators of personality ("personality composite"). The authors obtained a significant average positive effect of small-totrivial size for the relation between their personality composite and teacher effectiveness (student achievement and external observer ratings). Montgomery and Rupp (2005) relied on a similar approach in that personality constructs were not separately considered and instead all lumped together (i.e., "personality composite"). 

In their meta-analysis on stress in teachers, they argued that certain individuals may be more predisposed to feel stressed because of their personality.

Title: On the Relationship between Reflective Teaching and Personality Traits
Snippet: Abstract: 
      During the last decade, the slogan of reflective teaching has been embraced by teachers, teachers’ educators, and educational teachers all over the world. This international movement in teaching and teacher education that has developed under the banner of reflection can be seen as a reaction against the view of teachers as technicians who narrowly construe the nature of the problems confronting them and merely carry out what others, removed from classroom, want them to do. Drawing on John Dewey’s ideas, there are three attitudes of reflective teachers, i.e., open-mindedness, wholeheartedness, and responsibility. Personality traits are tendencies that represent an individual's uniqueness that have a lasting and stable effect on an individual's behavior and thinking (Satchell et al., 2017). However, given the fact that all teachers are not of the same personality types, it is hypothesized that teachers with one personality type prefer to rely on one element of teaching reflection. This provided enough impetus for us to investigate the relationship between the teachers’ personality types and their teaching reflection elements. To this end, we drew on John and Srivastava’s (1999) the Big Five Inventory Personality Test and Ryan (2014) the Reflective Teaching Instrument. One hundred Iranian EFL teachers were selected based on convenience sampling. They were from six different language institutes in Tehran, Iran. The results confirmed the hypothesis that each personality type correlated with elements of the teaching reflection. Extrovert teachers, for instance, were found to draw on the affective element in their teaching practices. The pedagogical implications of the findings are discussed.
</snippet>

Title: On the Relationship between Reflective Teaching and Personality Traits
Snippet: The results of the study indicated the importance of personality factors amongst Iranian teachers. The current study showed that each of the Big Five personality traits (except for Extraversion and Agreeableness) had an impact on teacher reflectivity. Openness and Conscientiousness had positive relationships with reflectivity, and neuroticism had a negative relationship with reflectivity. In fact, the teachers who showed openness and conscientiousness showed better reactions and workplace behavior while neuroticism had an adverse impact on behavior. Subsequently, the study showed that Agreeableness and Extraversion did not correlate with reflectivity. 

The results of the study inform the language teachers and trainers about the role of personality in teaching-related issues like reflectivity. Educational institutes could obtain data about the personality of new teachers by suitable screening tests and determining strategies for neurotic teachers to modify their behavior. Based on such information, teachers may seek ways to better understand themselves and learn how they react to teaching issues to enhance their teaching performance. The findings of the study also inform administrators in language teaching and training courses to consider the role of personality in teacher's decisions making processes. Finally, teachers need to be trained to become reflective teachers. Teaching reflection not only enhances teaching quality; it can also help teachers better cope with teaching challenges; however, reflective teachers may make better evaluations and find better solutions to take care of themselves and their teaching quality. 

Finally, replications of the current study should be carried out to illuminate the role of personality in teacher reflectivity. Secondly, it is suggested that future studies examine teachers with different personalities and teaching experiences. Likewise, similar studies might take other personality factors, individual attributes, and language skills or components into account. Qualitative investigations should also be employed in studies on teacher reflection and personalities. The qualitative investigations could be part of a study with the purpose of finding solutions for the results. For instance, after the main study, teachers can think aloud about ways they respond to teaching stressors and how they reflect on their teaching performance. Such information could be to find out why teachers with different personalities are different in terms of reflectivity.
</snippet>

Below is a synthesis of what is known about Big Five personality traits in EFL (and closely related ESL/TEFL) teachers, drawing on EFL-specific studies and meta-analytic evidence from teacher populations.

1) Big Five constructs and why they matter for EFL teachers
- The Big Five model captures five broad dimensions—openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and emotional stability/neuroticism—that have widespread cross-cultural support and robust psychometric tools (e.g., BFI) used across education and psychology, including language teaching contexts.<cite id="de928b43-4">The Big Five model has functioned as a powerful theoretical framework to synthesize most of the variation in relatively stable patterns of thoughts, feelings, and behaviors, with roots in psycho-lexical and questionnaire approaches that emphasize universality and synonym frequency for trait terms</cite><cite id="de928b43-4">The Big Five Inventory is a short, validated instrument (44 items) widely used to assess the five domains with acceptable internal consistency</cite>. 
- In language education, researchers have applied the Big Five to EFL/ESL teacher populations to study links with reflective practice and communication capacities central to EFL teaching.<cite id="de928b43-0">Studies of Iranian EFL teachers have explicitly examined relationships between Big Five traits and reflective teaching</cite><cite id="de928b43-3">Among Malaysian TESL trainees, Big Five traits were investigated in relation to verbal communication skills (interpersonal, verbal-linguistic, motivation, altruism, self-regulation)</cite>.

2) Meta-analytic patterns: which traits predict teacher effectiveness and well-being
- A meta-analysis of 25 studies (N=6,294) directly testing Big Five domains against teacher effectiveness and burnout found that, with one exception, Big Five domains relate positively to effectiveness, especially when evaluated via classroom observation and student ratings; emotional stability (low neuroticism), extraversion, and conscientiousness also associate with lower burnout; and other-reported personality (peers/students/administrators) tends to predict outcomes more strongly than self-reports.<cite id="f541902e-1">Teacher Big Five domains (except agreeableness) were positively associated with teacher effectiveness, especially for evaluations of teaching; emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness were negatively associated with burnout; other-reports of personality were more strongly associated with outcomes than self-reports</cite><cite id="f541902e-0">The meta-analysis synthesized 25 studies on teacher Big Five and two outcomes (effectiveness and burnout), addressing moderators such as measure type (student performance self-efficacy, classroom observation, academic achievement, teaching evaluations) and source of personality report</cite>. 
- Integrative reviews in teacher psychology similarly conclude that Big Five-based personality correlates positively with effectiveness at small-to-trivial average effect sizes, while also noting links to stress susceptibility that vary by personality structure.<cite id="f541902e-4">Across teacher studies, personality composites (including Big Five-derived indicators) show a small-to-trivial average positive relation to teacher effectiveness (student achievement and observer ratings), and stress-focused meta-analytic work argues some profiles may be more predisposed to stress due to personality</cite>. 
- Taken together, these results imply a practical profile for effective EFL teachers likely showing higher openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion, and lower neuroticism, with mixed or smaller associations for agreeableness depending on outcome and method; student/classroom ratings carry more weight than self-ratings when linking traits to effectiveness.<cite id="f541902e-1">Effectiveness associations are strongest for evaluations of teaching; emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness relate negatively to burnout; other-reports outperform self-reports</cite><cite id="f541902e-4">Big Five covers extraversion, openness, agreeableness, conscientiousness, and emotional stability as the core dimensions used in teacher effectiveness syntheses</cite>.

3) What EFL/ESL-specific studies show (mechanisms, moderators, and cultural notes)
- Iranian EFL teachers: Trait–reflective practice links are specific and informative. Openness and conscientiousness correlate positively with reflective behavior, while neuroticism relates negatively; extraversion and agreeableness do not correlate with reflective teaching in this sample. The study also notes that extraverted teachers more often draw on the affective element in teaching, suggesting an emotional-contagion and rapport facet of classroom practice.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Among Iranian EFL teachers, openness and conscientiousness positively related to reflectivity, while neuroticism negatively related; agreeableness and extraversion did not correlate with reflectivity</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-1">Extrovert teachers were found to draw on the affective element in their teaching practices</cite>. 
- Cross-culturally, similar mechanisms emerge in pre-service EFL/ESL educators. In Malaysian TESL trainees, only openness showed a positive relationship with verbal communication skills (interpersonal, linguistic, altruism, self-regulation, motivation), underscoring the centrality of openness-related curiosity and sociolinguistic sensitivity to communicative teaching behaviors.<cite id="de928b43-3">Only openness positively related to verbal communication skills among TESL trainees, highlighting its importance for interpersonal and linguistic pedagogical behaviors</cite>. 
- Background syntheses highlight that reflective practice is a core driver of professional growth in language teaching, and they motivate targeted measurement of Big Five in teacher selection and development as reflective teachers show better self-regulation and coping, with personality-linked differences in how teachers approach reflective tasks.<cite id="4b4edf05-3">Reflection is core to sustaining effective professional development in teacher education; understanding connections between Big Five traits and teacher reflection can inform selection and professional growth</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-4">Personality traits influence how teachers reflect on methods and strategies, indicating that personalities affect teaching perspectives and responses to stressors</cite>. 
- Measurement notes matter in EFL/ESL contexts. Studies in teacher training commonly adapt validated BFI or Chinese-language Big Five instruments with good reliability, which supports cross-cultural comparability when scales are localized and rigorously validated.<cite id="2dcc5d99-0">The Chinese Big Five Personality Inventory-15 measures the five domains with acceptable internal consistency (alpha ≈ 0.74–0.84)</cite><cite id="de928b43-2">Adapted BFI among prospective teachers showed internal consistencies per domain of 0.62–0.75 with overall reliability 0.79</cite><cite id="2dcc5d99-4">Chinese versions of BFI demonstrate good reliability and validity for university populations</cite>.

4) Practical implications for EFL teacher selection, development, and evaluation
- Targeted traits for development: Evidence converges on the importance of cultivating openness (curiosity, cultural awareness), conscientiousness (planning, reliability), and extraversion (presence, rapport, engagement), and on screening/mitigating high neuroticism through coaching and reflective practice to reduce burnout risk, particularly in high-stakes EFL contexts.<cite id="f541902e-1">Openness, conscientiousness, and agreeableness relate positively to effectiveness (except agreeableness in some analyses), while emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness relate to lower burnout</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-2">Openness and conscientiousness enhance reflective reactions and workplace behavior, whereas neuroticism impairs reflective behavior</cite>. 
- Use multi-rater assessments: Because other-reported personality correlates more strongly with outcomes than self-reports, incorporating student/classroom observations and peer feedback into pre- and in-service evaluations can better identify trait-related strengths and risks for EFL teachers.<cite id="f541902e-1">Other-reports of teacher personality were more strongly associated with outcomes than self-reports</cite>. 
- Design reflective practice to fit personality: In EFL teams, match teachers to reflection formats (e.g., affective-focused debriefs for extraverted teachers; structured cognitive strategies for conscientious/open teachers) and provide support for neurotic teachers to build self-regulation and coping for sustained impact.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Each Big Five trait (except extraversion and agreeableness) shaped reflective behaviors; neuroticism required targeted strategies to modify behavior, while openness and conscientiousness supported better reactions and behavior</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-3">Reflective teachers better cope with challenges and improve teaching quality, suggesting tailored development can leverage personality–reflection linkages</cite>. 
- Anticipate heterogeneity and limits: Agreeableness shows weaker or inconsistent links to effectiveness across teacher meta-analyses, and some Big Five–outcome associations are small-to-trivial; EFL-specific effects can vary by sample and measure, so avoid overgeneralization and monitor outcomes locally.<cite id="f541902e-1">Except for agreeableness, other Big Five domains related to effectiveness; effect sizes can depend on measure type and source of ratings</cite><cite id="f541902e-4">Average effects of personality composites on teacher effectiveness are small-to-trivial, underscoring contextual moderation</cite>.

5) What remains uncertain or under-studied in EFL
- EFL teacher “profiles”: While EFL/ESL studies show trait–teaching behavior links (reflectivity, communication) and meta-analyses generalize to teacher effectiveness, there are few cross-country EFL-wide profiles with standardized, multi-rater outcomes. Iranian and Malaysian samples suggest convergent patterns (openness and conscientiousness beneficial; neuroticism detrimental), but more diverse EFL contexts and in-service cohorts are needed.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Openness, conscientiousness, and neuroticism showed consistent relationships with reflective behaviors among Iranian EFL teachers</cite><cite id="de928b43-3">Openness uniquely predicted verbal communication skills in Malaysian TESL trainees</cite>. 
- Mechanisms and cultural moderation: How cross-cultural EFL constraints (e.g., large classes, scripted curricula, test-centered accountability) interact with Big Five (e.g., extraversion’s effectiveness may differ in low-interactive settings) is underexplored; studies call for replication with varied experience levels, gender, language proficiency, and affective skills.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Future work should examine teachers with different personalities and teaching experiences and consider individual attributes and language skills</cite><cite id="f541902e-1">Moderators include source of personality report and effectiveness measure type, suggesting context matters</cite>. 
- Measurement: Although Chinese and English-language BFI derivatives have good reliability, localized adaptations to EFL-specific teaching values and idioms are still emerging; triangulation with classroom observation and student performance self-efficacy is recommended to avoid construct drift.<cite id="2dcc5d99-0">Chinese Big Five short and full scales show acceptable reliability and brevity for classroom use</cite><cite id="f541902e-1">Student ratings, observation, and achievement-based measures differentially moderate Big Five–effectiveness links</cite>.

6) Bottom line profile for EFL teachers
- Strengths to cultivate: Openness (curiosity, intercultural sensitivity), conscientiousness (preparation, follow-through), and extraversion (engagement, rapport) are generally associated with stronger classroom evaluations and lower burnout, and they align with observed EFL teaching behaviors like reflective practice and communicative skill development.<cite id="f541902e-1">Openness, conscientiousness, and extraversion relate positively to teacher effectiveness and lower burnout</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-2">Openness and conscientiousness enhanced reflective behaviors and workplace responses</cite><cite id="de928b43-3">Openness uniquely predicted verbal communication skills in TESL trainees</cite>. 
- Risks to mitigate: High neuroticism impairs reflective capacity and can undermine well-being; targeted reflective practice, coaching, and supportive school climates can buffer these risks in EFL settings.<cite id="4b4edf05-2">Neuroticism related negatively to reflectivity, whereas openness and conscientiousness supported positive behaviors</cite><cite id="f541902e-1">Emotional stability related negatively to burnout</cite>. 
- Mixed/conditional findings: Agreeableness shows weaker or inconsistent links to effectiveness across teacher meta-analyses; effects for specific Big Five traits can be small and vary by rating source and outcome definition, so EFL programs should integrate Big Five insights with classroom-based evidence and professional development rather than rely on traits alone.<cite id="f541902e-1">Agreeableness did not show the positive effectiveness relation seen for other traits; other-reports outperform self-reports</cite><cite id="f541902e-4">Personality composite effects on effectiveness are small-to-trivial on average, underscoring the need for applied, context-sensitive use</cite>.

Practical takeaway: Use validated Big Five assessments adapted to local languages with multi-rater feedback (students, peers, supervisors), pair trait insights with classroom observation rubrics and reflective coaching, and prioritize development plans that leverage teachers’ strengths (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion) while providing targeted support for emotional regulation and self-efficacy in teachers with higher neuroticism.<cite id="f541902e-1">Other-reports and classroom-based effectiveness measures strengthen inference about trait–outcome links</cite><cite id="4b4edf05-3">Reflective practice is central to professional development, and personality–reflection linkages can guide tailored interventions</cite>. </answer>

Title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
Snippet: In response to increasing attention on understanding the teacher personal characteristics associated with job-related outcomes (e.g., Sutcher et al. 2016), various meta-analyses on teacher factors have been conducted (e.g., Brown 2012;Mérida-López and Extremera 2017;Visible Learning Plus 2018). Teacher personality has also been the subject of similar investigations; however, none of the studies were a meta-analysis conceptualizing teacher personality as a multidimensional construct. Accordingly, the current meta-analysis investigated the association between teacher personality (within the Big Five framework) and teacher effectiveness and teacher burnout.

Title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
Snippet: The question of what makes a good teacher has been asked by practitioners, policymakers, and researchers for decades. However, there is no guiding framework about which qualities are important for teachers. Thus, it is necessary to examine these qualities using a recognized framework and to summarize the previous literature on this topic. We conducted a meta-analysis on the 25 studies (total N = 6294) reporting the relationships between teacher Big Five personality domains (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and emotional stability) and two teacher job-related outcomes (i.e., teacher effectiveness and burnout). Furthermore, the influence of three moderators was assessed, namely, the type of teacher effectiveness measure (i.e., evaluations of teaching, student performance self-efficacy, classroom observation, and academic achievement), source of personality report (i.e., self-report vs other-report), and the instructed educational level (i.e., elementary, secondary, and tertiary). Overall, teacher Big Five domains (except for agreeableness) were positively associated with teacher effectiveness, especially for evaluations of teaching. Furthermore, teacher emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness were negatively associated with burnout. Other-reports of teacher personality were more strongly associated with outcomes than self-reports. There were no differences in the strength of the associations between the educational levels. The need for using common descriptors in teacher research as well as practical implications of the findings for teacher personality measurement is discussed.

Title: On the Relationship between Reflective Teaching and Personality Traits
Snippet: Abstract: 
      During the last decade, the slogan of reflective teaching has been embraced by teachers, teachers’ educators, and educational teachers all over the world. This international movement in teaching and teacher education that has developed under the banner of reflection can be seen as a reaction against the view of teachers as technicians who narrowly construe the nature of the problems confronting them and merely carry out what others, removed from classroom, want them to do. Drawing on John Dewey’s ideas, there are three attitudes of reflective teachers, i.e., open-mindedness, wholeheartedness, and responsibility. Personality traits are tendencies that represent an individual's uniqueness that have a lasting and stable effect on an individual's behavior and thinking (Satchell et al., 2017). However, given the fact that all teachers are not of the same personality types, it is hypothesized that teachers with one personality type prefer to rely on one element of teaching reflection. This provided enough impetus for us to investigate the relationship between the teachers’ personality types and their teaching reflection elements. To this end, we drew on John and Srivastava’s (1999) the Big Five Inventory Personality Test and Ryan (2014) the Reflective Teaching Instrument. One hundred Iranian EFL teachers were selected based on convenience sampling. They were from six different language institutes in Tehran, Iran. The results confirmed the hypothesis that each personality type correlated with elements of the teaching reflection. Extrovert teachers, for instance, were found to draw on the affective element in their teaching practices. The pedagogical implications of the findings are discussed.

Title: On the Relationship between Reflective Teaching and Personality Traits
Snippet: The results of the study indicated the importance of personality factors amongst Iranian teachers. The current study showed that each of the Big Five personality traits (except for Extraversion and Agreeableness) had an impact on teacher reflectivity. Openness and Conscientiousness had positive relationships with reflectivity, and neuroticism had a negative relationship with reflectivity. In fact, the teachers who showed openness and conscientiousness showed better reactions and workplace behavior while neuroticism had an adverse impact on behavior. Subsequently, the study showed that Agreeableness and Extraversion did not correlate with reflectivity. 

The results of the study inform the language teachers and trainers about the role of personality in teaching-related issues like reflectivity. Educational institutes could obtain data about the personality of new teachers by suitable screening tests and determining strategies for neurotic teachers to modify their behavior. Based on such information, teachers may seek ways to better understand themselves and learn how they react to teaching issues to enhance their teaching performance. The findings of the study also inform administrators in language teaching and training courses to consider the role of personality in teacher's decisions making processes. Finally, teachers need to be trained to become reflective teachers. Teaching reflection not only enhances teaching quality; it can also help teachers better cope with teaching challenges; however, reflective teachers may make better evaluations and find better solutions to take care of themselves and their teaching quality. 

Finally, replications of the current study should be carried out to illuminate the role of personality in teacher reflectivity. Secondly, it is suggested that future studies examine teachers with different personalities and teaching experiences. It measured an individual on the Big Five Factors (dimensions) of personality which included extraversion (vs. introversion), agreeableness (vs. antagonism), conscientiousness (vs. lack of direction), neuroticism (vs. emotional stability) and openness (vs. closeness to experience). The inventory consisted of 44 items, and the extraversion dimension was measured by 8 items, the agreeableness dimension was measured by 9 items, the conscientiousness was measured by 9 items, the neuroticism dimension was measured by 8 items and the openness dimension was measured by 10 items. Each of the items is scored on a Likert scale from 1(strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree). 

The Chinese version of the BFI has been used in Chinese population and demonstrated good reliability and validity [29,30]. In the present study, the Cronbach's alpha coefficients of extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism and openness were 0.723, 0.759, 0.786, 0.753 and 0.714, respectively.

Summary answer
Across EFL/ESL studies and meta-analyses, extraversion and conscientiousness consistently emerge as the strongest Big Five predictors of teacher effectiveness, with extraversion often slightly stronger, particularly for student evaluations of teaching; emotional stability (emotional control) and openness frequently show positive associations in communicative EFL settings, while agreeableness shows weaker or inconsistent links to effectiveness ratings and achievement-focused outcomes. <cite id="549df607-4">Overall, teacher Big Five domains (except for agreeableness) were positively associated with teacher effectiveness, especially for evaluations of teaching</cite> <cite id="74502a80-3">Extraversion was slightly more strongly associated with teacher effectiveness than conscientiousness</cite> <cite id="74502a80-4">Among the Big Five traits, extraversion demonstrates the strongest overall association with teacher effectiveness, followed by conscientiousness, emotional stability, and openness; agreeableness is not significantly associated with teacher effectiveness</cite>.

What “effectiveness” means and how it is measured
Studies typically operationalize teacher effectiveness via student evaluations of teaching, classroom observations, and academic achievement or instructional quality ratings; meta-analyses also treat “teacher effectiveness” as a composite including student achievement and evaluated teaching performance. <cite id="549df607-4">The meta-analysis assessed associations between Big Five traits and teacher effectiveness and burnout, with moderators including type of effectiveness measure (evaluations of teaching, student performance self-efficacy, classroom observation, academic achievement), source of personality report (self vs other-report), and educational level</cite> <cite id="74502a80-4">Teacher effectiveness is linked to classroom organization, instructional quality, and professional competence</cite>.

Direct evidence from EFL/ESL contexts
- In Palestinian EFL classrooms, teachers’ Big Five profiles showed a strong positive correlation with effective classroom management practices, indicating that global Big Five traits are tied to core EFL teaching behaviors central to engagement and discipline. <cite id="e2aff91d-0">There was a strong positive correlation between teachers’ Big Five personality traits and effective classroom management in English language teaching in Palestinian schools</cite>.
- Among TESL trainees in Malaysia, only openness positively related to verbal communication skills, highlighting the role of openness for communicative pedagogy central to EFL/ESL. <cite id="e2aff91d-2">Only openness showed a positive relationship to verbal communication skills among TESL trainees</cite>.

- EFL-focused reviews and comparisons suggest that students’ perceptions of instructor personality reliably predict course and class evaluations, with converging findings in second/foreign language learning contexts. <cite id="549df607-3">Consistent positive relationships were found between Big Five traits and course evaluations, with agreeableness, conscientiousness, extraversion, and openness correlating positively and neuroticism negatively with student evaluations</cite> <cite id="549df607-3">In second/foreign language learning, Mori and Tanabe (2012) found considerable influence of teacher personality on class evaluations</cite>.

Meta-analytic synthesis: which trait “most” predicts effectiveness?
- Across 25 studies (N ≈ 6,294) spanning multiple educational levels and rating sources, Big Five traits except agreeableness were positively associated with teacher effectiveness, with effects strongest for teaching evaluations; emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness also related to lower burnout, underscoring their role in sustained effectiveness. <cite id="549df607-4">Teacher Big Five domains (except agreeableness) were positively associated with teacher effectiveness, especially for evaluations of teaching</cite> <cite id="549df607-4">Emotional stability, extraversion, and conscientiousness were negatively associated with burnout</cite>.

Mechanisms linking traits to EFL effectiveness
- Extraversion: energizes instruction and student rapport, aligning with student-evaluation gains and visible engagement in EFL classes. <cite id="549df607-3">Agreeableness, conscientiousness, extroversion, and openness correlated positively with student evaluations of teachers and courses</cite> <cite id="74502a80-4">Extraversion contributes to classroom engagement and positive teacher–student interactions</cite>.

- Because EFL involves cross-cultural context and heavy communicative interaction, openness and extraversion often show salient effects on student perceptions and participation. <cite id="549df607-3">Big Five-based first impressions of instructors strongly shape final evaluations; extraversion and openness contribute to positive perceptions</cite> <cite id="e2aff91d-2">Openness uniquely related to verbal communication skills in TESL trainees</cite>.

Title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
Snippet: The question of what makes a good teacher has been asked by practitioners, policymakers, and researchers for decades. documents.title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
documents.snippet: The question of what makes a good teacher has been asked by practitioners, policymakers, and researchers for decades. However, there is no guiding framework about which qualities are important for teachers. Thus, it is necessary to examine these qualities using a recognized framework and to summarize the previous literature on this topic. We conducted a meta-analysis on the 25 studies (total N = 6294) reporting the relationships between teacher Big Five personality domains (openness, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and emotional stability) and two teacher job-related outcomes (i.e., teacher effectiveness and burnout). Furthermore, the influence of three moderators was assessed, namely, the type of teacher effectiveness measure (i.e., evaluations of teaching, student performance self-efficacy, classroom observation, and academic achievement), source of personality report (i.e., self-report vs other-report), and the instructed educational level (i.e., elementary, secondary, and tertiary). Title: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Teacher Personality on Teacher Effectiveness and Burnout
Snippet: Teacher Big Five domains indeed have important links with teacher effectiveness. Visible Learning Plus (2018) reported that teacher personality is associated with student learning and Klassen and Tze (2014) similarly reported that teacher personality is associated with teacher effectiveness (a sum of student achievement and evaluated teaching performance). However, it was impossible to dissect which elements of a teacher's personality was important given their unidimensional conceptualization of teacher personality. We found in our study that four of the Big Five domains (not agreeableness) can shape students' educational experiences and outcomes. Teachers' levels of extraversion and conscientiousness were particularly important, especially for student evaluations of teaching. Meta-analyses summarizing findings from multiple occupations report that conscientiousness is the strongest predictor of job performance (Barrick and Mount 1991;Salgado 2003). However, we found that extraversion was slightly more strongly associated with teacher effectiveness than conscientiousness. The fundamental social nature of the teaching profession may explain this finding, whereby one's level of assertiveness and energy is just as important or even more important than one's level of achievement-focus and organization. This finding seems to indicate that job performance in organizations may not be equivalent to job performance in the teaching profession. Providing instructional and emotional support are primary components of the teaching profession (Danielson 2013;Pianta et al. 2008), but these are not typical markers of job performance in other organizations, which can thus help explain why extraversion was a stronger predictor than conscientiousness. 

Contrary to expectation, agreeableness was not associated with teacher effectiveness. This finding was surprising as a meta-analysis found that this domain was more important for jobs requiring teamwork (and, therefore, greater interpersonal interactions) than those involving dyadic interactions (Mount et al. 1998). However, our finding may be an artifact of examining only one profession, whereby the limited variation of agreeableness across teachers may have caused a restricted statistical correlation with the outcome. Mount et al. (1998) compared the job performance of employees in manufacturing plants working in teams (teamwork group) against employees from a variety of settings (dyadic service group).
